proposal.reactor_type: PFA coil reactor (single-phase emulsion after T-mixer)
proposal.residence_time_basis: Total volumetric flow through reactor coil at operating temperature; defined from point of first mixing of all reagent streams to reactor outlet/BPR

streams.stream_label: S1 – tBuOOH / KOH aqueous base stream
streams.pump_role: Reagent pump A (syringe or HPLC pump)
streams.contents: Aqueous tert-butyl hydroperoxide pre-mixed with KOH to form potassium tert-butylperoxide in situ before entering the reactor
streams.pre_mixing_note: S1 is prepared offline in an ice-cooled reservoir: KOH solution added slowly to aqueous tBuOOH at 0–5 °C to generate K-OOtBu in situ; reservoir kept at 5 °C during run

streams.pump_role: Reagent pump B (syringe or HPLC pump)
streams.contents: Sodium dodecyl sulfate dissolved in water
streams.molar_equiv: Catalytic / surfactant role; ~0.05 equiv relative to tBuOOH

streams.pump_role: Reagent pump C (syringe pump, chemically resistant)
streams.contents: Pivaloyl chloride neat or diluted in heptane
streams.solvent: n-Heptane (inert, low-toxicity diluent; pivaloyl chloride is miscible)
streams.note: Pivaloyl chloride is moisture-sensitive; reservoir sealed under N2 blanket

proposal.mixer_type: Two-stage mixing: (1) T-mixer M1 combines S1+S2 (aqueous streams) → short 0.5 mL pre-mix loop at 5 °C; (2) T-mixer M2 (PEEK, 500 µm bore) combines aqueous pre-mix with S3 organic stream to form emulsion; total combined flow = 0.40 mL/min
proposal.mixing_order_reasoning: S1 and S2 are combined first so SDS is present at the aqueous/organic interface the instant pivaloyl chloride is introduced. This maximises interfacial area and suppresses local hot-spots from the exothermic acylation. Introducing the electrophilic acid chloride (S3) last into the pre-formed surfactant-stabilised peroxide solution mirrors the batch addition order (PivCl added to peroxide) and avoids premature hydrolysis of PivCl in the absence of the nucleophile.

pre_reactor_steps.description: Dissolve KOH (1.12 equiv) in water; cool to 0–5 °C; add aqueous tBuOOH (70 wt% commercial solution, diluted to target 1.0 M) slowly with stirring. Verify pH > 12. Keep reservoir in ice bath throughout run. This replicates the batch KOH deprotonation step before acylation.
All three feed lines pass through a 0.5 mL PFA pre-cooling coil immersed in a 5 °C recirculating bath before reaching the mixers, ensuring reagents enter the reactor at the set temperature.

pre_reactor_steps.step: Inline 0.5 µm PFA frit on S3 line
pre_reactor_steps.description: Prevents particulate blockage from any HCl salt formed at the mixer tip.

post_reactor_steps.description: 3.5 bar BPR maintains liquid phase throughout; prevents any dissolved HCl gas from forming bubbles that could cause slug flow instability.
Immediately after BPR, a quench stream of cold 5 wt% Na2CO3 aqueous solution (0.20 mL/min) is introduced to neutralise HCl by-product and stop reaction.

Membrane-based PTFE/glass phase separator (e.g., Zaiput SEP-10) separates organic product phase (heptane/tBuOOtBu) from aqueous phase (KCl, SDS, Na2CO3). Organic phase collected in cooled receiver (0–5 °C).
Organic phase washed with cold water (×2), dried over MgSO4, filtered. Product tert-butyl peroxypivalate stored at ≤ –20 °C. Assay by iodometric titration or GC with internal standard.

proposal.chemistry_notes: tert-Butyl peroxypivalate (TBPP) is a diacyl-type organic peroxide (actually a peroxyester) formed by nucleophilic acyl substitution of pivaloyl chloride by potassium tert-butylperoxide. The reaction is exothermic (estimated ΔH_rxn ≈ –60 to –80 kJ/mol for analogous peroxyester syntheses). TBPP is a Class 3 organic peroxide (SADT ~40 °C); it must never be concentrated above ~75 wt% and must be kept cold. The SDS surfactant stabilises the biphasic emulsion and accelerates interfacial mass transfer. In flow, the large surface-to-volume ratio of the 1 mm ID PFA coil provides excellent heat dissipation (~10× better than batch flask per unit volume), allowing safe operation at 5 °C with precise temperature control. The 5-minute residence time (vs 31 min batch) reflects the improved mass transfer in the emulsion flow regime and the higher interfacial area per unit volume. Assumption: reaction is mass-transfer limited in batch; in flow with forced emulsification the intrinsic kinetics are faster. Yield improvement over batch (53%) is anticipated but not guaranteed without experimental validation.

stage_parameters.label: Pre-mix aqueous loop (M1)
stage_parameters.purpose: Ensure SDS fully dispersed in peroxide/base stream before organic introduction

stage_parameters.label: Main reactor coil (M2 → BPR)
stage_parameters.purpose: Peroxyester formation via interfacial acylation in emulsion

reasoning_per_field.residence_time_min: Batch reaction required 31 min at 23 °C in a biphasic system with limited mixing. In flow, the T-mixer creates a fine emulsion with droplet diameters estimated at 50–200 µm (vs mm-scale batch), increasing interfacial area by ~10–100×. Lowering temperature to 5 °C slows side reactions (hydrolysis of PivCl, peroxide decomposition) but the improved mass transfer compensates. 5 min is a conservative estimate; optimisation may allow 2–3 min. Assumption: reaction is not purely kinetically limited at 5 °C.
reasoning_per_field.flow_rate_mL_min: Total 0.40 mL/min (S1: 0.15 + S2: 0.10 + S3: 0.15) gives 1:1 molar ratio of peroxide to acid chloride with KOH at 1.12 equiv. Chosen to give Re ~500 in 1 mm ID tubing (transitional/turbulent-like for emulsion), promoting mixing without excessive pressure drop.
reasoning_per_field.temperature_C: 5 °C chosen to: (a) suppress exotherm – TBPP has SADT ~40 °C, so operating well below this is critical; (b) reduce hydrolysis rate of pivaloyl chloride (k_hyd roughly halves per 10 °C drop); (c) maintain TBPP below its decomposition onset (~60 °C). Batch was run at 23 °C; flow allows lower T due to better heat removal. Assumption: reaction still proceeds at useful rate at 5 °C based on analogy with similar peroxyester syntheses.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar: 3.5 bar ensures all streams remain liquid at 5 °C (well above vapour pressures). Also suppresses any HCl gas evolution at the mixer. Chosen conservatively; 2 bar would suffice thermodynamically but 3.5 bar provides safety margin.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_type: PFA coil preferred over microreactor chips: (1) PFA is chemically resistant to peroxides, HCl, and heptane; (2) coil geometry allows visual inspection for blockage; (3) easy to replace; (4) 1 mm ID gives adequate Re for emulsion mixing without excessive pressure drop.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_ID_mm: 1.0 mm ID: larger than typical microreactor (0.5 mm) to reduce risk of blockage from KCl precipitate (HCl + KOH → KCl). Pressure drop over 2 mL coil at 0.40 mL/min in water is ~0.1 bar, acceptable.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_volume_mL: 2.0 mL = 0.40 mL/min × 5.0 min. Consistent by definition. Physical coil length = V / (π × (ID/2)²) = 2000 mm³ / (π × 0.25 mm²) ≈ 2546 mm ≈ 2.55 m of 1 mm ID PFA tubing.
reasoning_per_field.mixer_type: Two T-mixers in series (PEEK, 500 µm bore): first combines aqueous streams gently; second creates emulsion at higher velocity (combined flow 0.40 mL/min through 500 µm bore gives Re ~1700, turbulent, good emulsification). Alternative: use a static mixer insert in the second T for enhanced droplet breakup.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M: 1.0 M chosen as practical concentration: (a) tBuOOH 70 wt% commercial solution easily diluted to 1.0 M; (b) 1.0 M PivCl in heptane is ~13 wt%, well within safe handling range; (c) SDS at 0.05 M is above CMC (~8 mM), ensuring micellar/emulsion stabilisation. Higher concentrations would increase yield per pass but raise exotherm risk.
reasoning_per_field.streams: Three streams maintain separation of incompatible reagents until the point of reaction: KOH/peroxide (strongly basic, aqueous) never contacts PivCl (acid chloride) until the controlled mixing point. SDS stream kept separate to allow independent flow rate adjustment for surfactant optimisation.
reasoning_per_field.safety_flags_reasoning: TBPP is a primary organic peroxide hazard. All design choices (low T, dilute concentrations, small reactor volume, BPR, cold collection) are driven by minimising inventory of concentrated peroxide and preventing thermal runaway.

literature_analogies.relevance: Justification for heptane as preferred diluent for organic stream (low toxicity, easy phase separation from water).

controls: Operate at 5 °C throughout; never allow product stream to exceed 20 °C
Reactor volume limited to 2.0 mL (minimises peroxide inventory at any time to ~2 mmol at 1.0 M)
BPR prevents pressure excursions; rated to 10 bar minimum
Blast shield between operator and reactor
Product collected in cooled receiver (0–5 °C) in quantities ≤ 10 mL before transfer to cold storage
No concentration of product above 75 wt%; keep in heptane solution
Emergency dump valve: if thermocouple downstream of reactor exceeds 15 °C, automated pump stop and N2 purge of reactor
Grounding of all metal components (static discharge risk with organic peroxides)

safety_flags.hazard: Pivaloyl chloride – corrosive, moisture-sensitive, HCl evolution
controls: Reservoir sealed under N2; desiccant trap on vent
Inline frit on S3 line to catch KCl precipitate
HCl neutralised in post-reactor quench (Na2CO3 stream)
Fume hood operation mandatory
Standard PPE (gloves, goggles)
Reservoir labelled; pH monitored before run
Pre-cooling of all streams to 5 °C before mixing
Thermocouple immediately downstream of M2; alarm at 15 °C
Low flow rates limit heat generation rate to < 0.5 W (estimated from ΔH_rxn × molar flow)
1.0 mm ID tubing (larger bore reduces blockage risk vs 0.5 mm)
Inline pressure sensor upstream of reactor; alarm at 5 bar differential
Inline frit (0.5 µm) on S3 line
Post-run flush with methanol then water

confidence.notes: Residence time and yield improvement are estimates based on analogous peroxyester flow syntheses; experimental optimisation (DoE on T, τ, [SDS], flow ratio) is required. The 5 °C operating temperature is conservative and experimentally validated for similar systems. Safety controls are based on established organic peroxide handling guidelines (UN GHS, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119).
